newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq readies partial oil sales after six-year ban.
newsitem.headline: Iraq readies partial oil sales after six-year ban.

text.p: Iraqi gained final U.N. clearance to begin pumping oil to world markets early on Tuesday for the first time since its exports were banned more than six years ago.

A celebration was scheduled at the oil centre of Kirkuk for 8 a.m. (0500 GMT) -- the midnight New York time set by the United Nations for Iraq to open the tap. Among those expected to attend was Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed.

The flow of the first Iraqi crude to international markets since President Saddam Hussein's troops invaded neighbouring Kuwait in August 1990, and the purchases of humanitarian goods with the proceeds, will be under tight U.N. monitoring.

The "oil-for-food" deal that Iraq accepted after earlier refusals will allow it to export $2 billion worth of oil in a six-month period to pay for humanitarian needs of its 20 million people suffering under economic sanctions.

At current prices, Iraq will be able to export slightly under 600,000 barrels of oil a day, most of it via a pipeline across Turkey and the rest through the Gulf. Before the Gulf War, it exported more than three million barrels a day.
Of the $2 billion earned, about $1.32 billion will go for humanitarian supplies, including $260 million for goods for the largely Kurdish-inhabited north of Iraq.
Of the remainder, $600 million will go to a U.N. fund to pay reparations to people who suffered losses in the 1990 invasion and 1991 Gulf War when Iraq was driven from Kuwait.

Another $20 million will go to the U.N. Special Commission in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, which must certify it has completed its work before Iraq can export oil freely. Administrative and operational costs account for most of the rest.
If all goes well, the Security Council may renew the deal when the initial six months expire.

An offer of limited exports was first made to Iraq in 1991 but Baghdad turned it down, saying the terms violated its sovereignty. The U.N. renewed the offer in 1995 and issued resolution 986 on which the partial exports are based.
Iraq again stalled but in February 1996 agreed to enter negotiations with the United Nations. On May 28 Iraqi and U.N. negotiators reached a memorandum of understanding.
Bickering over the number of U.N. food observers and how they would supervise distribution delayed its implementation.

It was about to be carried out in September but was put on hold when Baghdad backed one side in inter-Kurdish fighting in late August in the north of the country, an area its forces had been effectively barred from since 1991.
On November 27, Iraq accepted all U.N. terms to activate the deal.

The deal does not affect the overall ban on Iraqi oil exports, which cannot be lifted until the U.N. Special Commission says Baghdad has met all weapons requirements under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire terms.

Chief U.N. arms inspector Rolf Ekeus is in Baghdad trying to overcome Iraqi objections to taking the remains of missile engines out of Iraq for testing to prove they are real. He has charged that Iraq may still be hiding missiles.

But the imminent flow of oil overshadowed the latest in years of standoffs with U.N. arms inspectors. State-run radio, television and press herald the limited exports as the prelude to the removal of all sanctions on Iraq.
